I prefer to solve on paper* and with early week puzzles I'll read the clues but not write the answers right away.  I try to remember as many as possible and write them down all at once. *We paper solvers need to organize.  It has become far to common for the NYT staff to offer only the Newspaper version of the puzzle for printing and not publish the PDF or Large Print versions.  This usually is when there is some sort of graphic in the grid but yesterday's grid was standard.  I know we "dead tree" solvers are a minority but our subscription $$'s should still count.

Simple theme, yes, but beautifully presented.  The theme answers are colorful, the reveal is hard to guess without crosses or reading its clue (Hi, @ John Carson!), and HOOCH, SAUCE, and JUICE don’t use their “poison” meanings in their theme answers.

PICK YOUR POISON, by the way, is a Times answer debut, and furthermore, it has never appeared in any of the major crossword outlets.

Furthermore, the box contains beauty in answer, with PUMMEL, JUT OUT, AMBIT, DEBUNKS, and UPEND.

I also liked I’M UP starting on the top row, and ON EDGE starting on the top border.

So, much loveliness packed in the box today, making for a rich start to the week.  Dena, I’m glad you persisted in fine-tuning this after it was initially turned down, and thank you for a sweet solve!

Hello! Hope you’re all having a lovely Monday!

I do have some questions to my fellow crossword solvers. I’m not from an English-speaking country, so it’s taken me quite a while to get the hang of the crosswords. Mondays are finally starting to feel a bit more manageable, and sometimes even Tuesdays if I’m lucky. 
But I still rely quite a bit on autocheck and often have to look up clues. There are still days when the puzzles feel WAY too difficult, even though I’ve been doing them for quite a long time now.
So I’m curious, my fellow crossword solvers (especially those of you who aren’t native English speakers): how long did it take before you felt like you could solve, say, a Wednesday puzzle reasonably well?
I feel like I’ve completely hit a plateau!

Right? I thought from the start I was supposed to enter CDS there but it felt wrong. CDS are a physical medium of digital storage, while MP3 is a digital file format - those are two different classes of things. Books could be described as precursors of e-readers, maybe, but were books precursors of the EPUB file format? IMO not.

The first discs were Audio CD format (aka Red Book) which became popular in the early 80s. 

You're thinking of CD-R, CD-RW or CD-ROM, which can hold data files, including mp3s. The mp3 format didn't get invented until the mid 90s.

I think it's because, for a time, there were "MP3 Players" just as there were CD players.  The former was something of a misnomer in that it was potentially playing both at the same time (an Mp3 file burned to a CD).

"Were there other pop culture titles that could be confused thusly?"

These are more challenging puzzles for solvers who are not native (or very experienced) English speakers.  Word-play, puns, and colloquialisms/slang add to the issues.  (I am thinking of YUP and MASON Jar...)  
You are working on puzzles that are more difficult than most.  To me, it means you are doing very well.  Maybe others can point you to some puzzles that provide helpful practice...?

Although I am a native speaker of English, here's my experience.  When I started doing these puzzles regularly about twenty years ago I rarely even attempted the Friday and Saturday versions. They were just too frustrating. But over the years with practice came a number of realizations, perhaps the most important being in my view that the more difficult the puzzle the more likely its clues will have their own--je ne sais quoi--vibe?  Thing?  Schtick?  If you can get a sense of that, the solves will begin to fall into place.
I always do the L A Times puzzle as a warm up.

@Marte, I've been solving so long that I don't remember what the timeline was! I've been solving for about fifty years, starting as a teenager; I'm 66 now.

What I would say is this: it doesn't matter how long it takes to become proficient. If you're enjoying this addictive hobby, carry on! Use all the tools you need. There's a book I read to my third grade students; it's called The Magical Yet, by Angela Diterlizzi. It reminds us not to give up. Rather than saying, "I can't" say, " I can't do it YET."

Read the Wordplay column; it's probably the best tool you have. Sure, you can use Google, a dictionary, the answer key (and even after 50-ish years I sometimes need help!), but those just supply answers, not tips, tricks, and strategies. 

I give you props for solving in a language that's not your first. That's a huge challenge! I'm fluent in French to the degree that I dream in French, especially when in France (My spouse is French and we've raised two bilingual kids), but I claim no proficiency in crosswords in French! Their puzzle style/format is different and I've never taken the time to dig into it. Congrats and kudos to you. 

Welcome to the NYT crossword community!

As a retired ESL teacher, I would put crosswords at the top of the list of recommended activities for advanced English learners (with heavy emphasis on the word "advanced").  All the idioms, the homophones, homonyms, etc. come out to play; they are vocabulary goldmines, geography quizzes, cultural explorations and on and on.  If a learner can hold their own on Mondays and Tuesdays the rest will follow with time.  But I can't think of a better way to push the edge of the learning envelope.  You're in the right place.
@Marte  It definitely took a couple of years of practice for me.  I couldn't imagine doing these as a non-native English speaker.  Kudos to you!

It’s not the English language that’s going to trip you up; I was in Norway recently, and you guys all seem to know English quite well. It’s the American culture items: the movie stars, the sports terms, the old TV shows, etc. 

Immerse yourself in American pop culture as best you can, and it will pay dividends for your solving abilities.

It took about 12 or 18 months before I was able to solve most NYT puzzles on my own, including late week ones. The only way to progress, IMO, is to attempt to solve all puzzles, Saturdays, too, right from the start. At first you'll find them very hard, and you'll probably need to use autocheck for months. My first Saturday took 4 hours 😃
Also, there's way too much American culture out there for you to master it, so Steve L's advice above is Ioco. Just try to remember the recurring American stuff.
@Niall, I don't know how often it appears, but I agree that in everyday life, unless you're a linguist (or just a garden variety polyglot and word nerd, as I am) it's an obscure word.
Niall, ERSE may be the epitome of crosswordese if it is never heard in Ireland but has shown up 744 times in the grid. Here's the first appearance: https://www.xwordinfo.com/PS?date=3/1/1942&h=43d
ERSE does indeed show up here frequently, usually followed by complaints from those of the Gaelic persuasion that it's archaic at best, mildly offensive at worst. Yet here we are.

I'm sure you're right that ERSE is not used in everyday language, in Ireland or anywhere else these days, but no matter where you reside, the fact that you've never seen or heard a word before doesn't mean it can't be a valid entry.

ERSE is a very rare word, to be sure, and undoubtedly obsolete, but it's in all the dictionaries.  All with the same definition, same as the clue.  And while you might argue it has no place in a Monday crossword, and I might even agree with you, you can't argue that the clue is inaccurate.  Clues, even on Monday, do not require any indication that a word is rare, obscure, historical, outdated, obsolete, etc.

ERSE is a convenient word for constructors because it contains only extremely useful letters.  So it's crosswordese of the highest order, its frequency in puzzles far outstripping that in real life.
